summary:
Tonga's Criminal Offences Act criminalises same-sex activity between men and women, with a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment. Outright International's overview, updated in March 2026, records no evidence of enforcement in recent years, and the US State Department's 2010 human rights report described enforcement of the sodomy provision as rare.

The same statute contains an offence aimed squarely at gender expression: a male who solicits in public "for an immoral purpose" with intent to deceive as to his true sex commits an offence. This is a trans-expression provision on the books, and unlike the sodomy provision it turns on visible presentation rather than private conduct, so it bears directly on how a trans visitor may appear and speak in public spaces.

Tonga provides no legal gender recognition. A visitor's documents will therefore carry the sex marker assigned at birth, with no domestic mechanism to alter it, and no source in the inventory describes any screening process, entry form or facility rule that would accommodate a marker that does not match presentation.

Tongan law does not address discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment or in the provision of goods and services. The Judicial Code of Conduct 2010 requires judges to be aware of diversity including sexual orientation and prohibits bias on irrelevant grounds, but it binds judges alone, not employers or service providers, so it offers a visitor no practical recourse.

Tonga does not recognise same-sex sexual relationships or unions in any form. No partnership, marriage or next-of-kin rights appear in the source material, which matters for hospital access, emergency contact and inheritance in a country where a visitor's partner has no standing.

Violence risk is documented rather than theoretical. Polikalepo Kefu, a noted LGBTQ activist, was murdered near his home at Muʻa in 2021. The source material describes a climate of fear, discrimination and homophobia attributed to conservative values, colonial-era laws, and rising fundamentalism and religious fanaticism that has increased hatred towards LGBTQ people and fakaleitis.

Community infrastructure for LGBTQ people is thin and has been damaged. In February 2018 Cyclone Gita tore off part of the roof of Tonga's LGBTI drop-in center and shelter on Tongatapu in Nuku'alofa, with winds over 120 mph, damaging bathrooms and bedrooms used by LGBTI Tongans; the country's only such shelter.

Official posture offers little protection machinery. Tonga, along with Kiribati, is the only Polynesian country that has not signed or expressed support for the 2011 UN joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The 2010 US State Department report recorded no government abuses, while naming domestic violence, discrimination against women and corruption as the most prevalent human rights problems.
tangentialFactors:
Trans visibility in Tonga is not absent: a Washington Post feature of August 2024 covered a Tongan trans pageant and the wider LGBT rights situation, indicating an organised public trans presence alongside the legal hostility.

The legal regime is regional rather than unique in one respect only: Tonga and Kiribati stand apart in the subregion for declining to support the 2011 UN joint statement, while neighbouring Polynesian states have moved the other way.

The 2010 US State Department report framed Tonga's human rights picture around domestic violence, discrimination against women and corruption, with sodomy on the books but rarely enforced and no government abuses recorded. That report is now more than a decade old and its enforcement finding has not been refreshed by any court-level source in the inventory.

The UK Foreign Office travel advice for Tonga yielded no trans-specific or LGBT-specific finding usable for this record.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the same criminal provisions as visitors, with no domestic campaign in the source material recorded as having repealed the sodomy or trans-expression offences.

Employment and access to goods and services are unprotected on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity; the only anti-bias instrument cited, the Judicial Code of Conduct 2010, constrains judges and leaves employers and providers free to discriminate.

Same-sex couples have no partnership, marriage or next-of-kin standing, so property, hospital visitation and funeral decisions default to blood relatives.

The LGBTI drop-in center and shelter in Nuku'alofa is the country's sole community facility of its kind, and its 2018 cyclone damage illustrates how little redundancy exists in LGBTQ support infrastructure.

Social conditions are described as a climate of fear shaped by conservative religious values, colonial-era legislation and rising fundamentalism, with fakaleiti people specifically named as targets of increased hostility, and the 2021 killing of an LGBTQ activist at Muʻa as the sharpest recorded instance.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the trans-expression offence has ever been charged or prosecuted is unresolved: no source in the inventory reports a conviction, a charge or a stated enforcement policy for that provision, and the enforcement-rarity finding rests on a 2010 government report plus a 2026 NGO overview rather than court records.

No source addresses entry or visa screening, airport document checks, or whether a mismatch between a visitor's gender marker and presentation would be questioned at the border; this remains not sourced rather than confirmed absent.

Availability of gender-affirming healthcare, prescription-hormone rules and any local clinical gatekeeping are not sourced here, as is the position on restroom and facility access for trans visitors.

Whether Tonga would recognise a same-sex marriage or civil partnership obtained abroad is not stated in the source material and should be treated as unresolved.

The inventory contains no Tongan court decision, ministry statement or police data on hate-crime treatment of offences against LGBTQ people, and no source on whether any legal gender recognition process exists in draft or before parliament.
